families.title: Restart and improve
families.blurb: Build a solution, improve it locally, then shake it or start again.

families.title: Walk with an acceptance rule
families.blurb: Move from solution to solution and decide when a worse one is acceptable.

families.title: Destroy and repair
families.blurb: Tear out part of the solution and rebuild it.

families.title: Populations
families.blurb: Keep several solutions and combine what works.

families.title: Random-key baselines
families.blurb: Code a solution as numbers between 0 and 1 and let a general-purpose optimiser move them. They are included as baselines and ranked last in our screening campaigns.

heuristics.label: Ant colony optimisation
heuristics.title: Ant colony optimisation
heuristics.tagline: Ants build orders guided by pheromone
how: Each ant first picks how many depots to use, then which, with probabilities from pheromone and from closeness to the customers.
It then builds a customer order step by step: the next customer is drawn by pheromone times closeness.
The order is turned into routes by cheapest insertion.
Pheromone evaporates; the best fifth of the ants deposit new pheromone in proportion to 1 / cost on the depots and customer pairs they used.
refs: Dorigo, Maniezzo & Colorni (1996), IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics B 26:29–41
impl: This is not the savings-based ant system of the literature. The deposit is small against the start pheromone.
With a time limit the iteration cap has no effect.

heuristics.label: Adaptive large neighbourhood search
heuristics.title: Adaptive large neighbourhood search
heuristics.tagline: Like LNS, but learns which operator works
how: Same destroy and repair operators as LNS.
Each operator has a weight. The operators for an iteration are drawn in proportion to their weights.
An operator earns points: 5 for a new best solution, 2 for an improvement, 0.5 for an accepted worse solution.
Every 50 iterations the weights move toward the average points earned. Worse solutions are accepted by a cooling rule, as in simulated annealing.
refs: Ropke & Pisinger (2006), Transportation Science 40:455–472
impl: The scores, segment length and reaction factor differ from Ropke & Pisinger (2006); there is no insertion noise and the removal size is fixed.

heuristics.label: Biased random-key GA
heuristics.title: Biased random-key genetic algorithm
how: A solution is a vector of numbers in [0, 1]: one key per customer (their order), one per depot (their ranking) and one that sets how many depots may open.
A decoder sorts the keys and builds routes by cheapest insertion.
Each generation keeps the elite, adds a few fresh random vectors, and makes the rest as children that take each key from an elite parent with a set probability.
refs: Gonçalves & Resende (2011), Journal of Heuristics 17:487–525
impl: No local search in the default setup. With a time limit the generation cap has no effect.

heuristics.label: Random-key differential evolution
heuristics.title: Differential evolution (random keys)
how: The population is a set of random-key vectors, decoded as in BRKGA.
For each member, a mutant is built from three other members: a + F × (b − c), wrapped into [0, 1].
A trial vector takes each key from the mutant with probability CR, otherwise from the member.
The trial replaces the member if it decodes to a cheaper solution.
refs: Storn & Price (1997), Journal of Global Optimization 11:341–359
impl: No local search in the default setup. With a time limit the iteration cap has no effect.

heuristics.label: Genetic algorithm
heuristics.title: Genetic algorithm
heuristics.tagline: Crossover and mutation on customer orders
how: Create a population of randomised greedy solutions. Each one carries a customer order and a set of depots.
Pick two parents by tournament of three. Ordered crossover mixes their customer orders; the depot set comes from one parent and is sometimes changed by one depot.
Mutate the order, then rebuild routes by cheapest insertion in that order.
Copy the best few solutions unchanged into the next generation.
refs: Holland (1975), Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems
impl: With a time limit the generation cap has no effect: the algorithm runs until the deadline.

heuristics.label: GRASP
heuristics.title: GRASP (greedy randomised adaptive search)
heuristics.tagline: Randomised greedy builds, each improved locally
how: Build a solution by cheapest insertion, but pick at random among the few best insertion moves instead of always the best one.
Improve it with local search (first-descent in the default setup).
Keep it if it is the best so far, then build a new one from scratch.
Repeat until the time limit.
refs: Feo & Resende (1995), Journal of Global Optimization 6:109–133
Prins, Prodhon & Wolfler Calvo (2006), 4OR 4:221–238 (GRASP with learning and path relinking for the CLRP)
impl: Depots are decided only by the construction; the default local search has no depot move.
Each pass makes a fixed number of constructions, then a new pass starts.

heuristics.label: GRASP with path relinking
heuristics.title: GRASP with path relinking
heuristics.tagline: GRASP, plus walks toward elite solutions
how: Run GRASP: randomised greedy build, then local search.
Keep a small pool of the best different solutions found in this pass.
Walk from each new solution toward a random pool member: at every step try moving each out-of-place customer to its position in the target order, rebuild by cheapest insertion, and take the cheapest.
Keep the best point on the walk; add the result to the pool.
refs: Prins, Prodhon & Wolfler Calvo (2006), 4OR 4:221–238
impl: The pool is emptied at the start of every pass.
Relinking works on the customer order, not on the routes.

heuristics.label: Iterated greedy
heuristics.title: Iterated greedy
how: Start from a randomised greedy solution.
Remove a fixed share of the customers at random.
Reinsert them one by one at the cheapest position.
Keep the result only if it is better than the current solution.
refs: Ruiz & Stützle (2007), European Journal of Operational Research 177:2033–2049
impl: This is LNS reduced to one destroy operator (random) and one repair operator (greedy), without local search.

heuristics.label: Iterated local search
heuristics.title: Iterated local search
how: Build a start solution and improve it with local search.
Perturb it with a few random feasible moves.
Improve the perturbed solution; keep it only if it beats the current one.
After a fixed number of rounds, start again from a new construction.
refs: Lourenço, Martin & Stützle (2003), in Handbook of Metaheuristics, Springer
impl: A perturbation move can reassign a route to another depot or split a route, so depots can change here.

heuristics.label: Large neighbourhood search
heuristics.title: Large neighbourhood search
heuristics.tagline: Remove a part, rebuild it, keep if better
how: Start from a randomised greedy solution.
Destroy: remove a share of the customers, chosen at random, close to one random customer, or those whose removal saves the most.
Repair: put them back by cheapest insertion or by regret-2 insertion. A new route may start at any depot.
Keep the result only if it is better than the current solution.
refs: Shaw (1998), Principles and Practice of Constraint Programming, LNCS 1520:417–431
Pisinger & Ropke (2010), in Handbook of Metaheuristics, Springer
impl: The destroy and repair operators are drawn uniformly at random; nothing is learned.
Depots change only indirectly, when a repair starts a route at another depot.

heuristics.label: Multi-start local search
heuristics.title: Multi-start local search
how: Draw a random order of the customers.
Insert them one by one at the cheapest feasible position (ties broken at random).
Improve the result with local search.
Keep the best and draw a new order.
refs: Martí, Resende & Ribeiro (2013), European Journal of Operational Research 226:1–8
impl: Uses the same order-based decoder as the genetic, ant, swarm and random-key methods.
Depots are decided only by the decoder.

heuristics.label: Random-key PSO
heuristics.title: Particle swarm optimisation (random keys)
how: Each particle is a random-key vector, decoded as in BRKGA.
Its velocity combines its own momentum, a pull toward its own best position and a pull toward the swarm's best.
Positions wrap around inside [0, 1]. Personal and swarm bests are updated after each decode.
refs: Kennedy & Eberhart (1995), Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Neural Networks, 1942–1948
impl: No local search in the default setup. With a time limit the iteration cap has no effect.

heuristics.label: Random-key random search
heuristics.title: Random-key random search
how: Draw a random key vector.
Decode it with the same decoder as BRKGA, PSO and DE.
Keep the best solution seen. Nothing is learned between draws.
impl: A control for the three methods above: if they do not beat it, their search is not helping.
With a time limit the trial cap has no effect.

heuristics.label: Simulated annealing
heuristics.title: Simulated annealing
heuristics.tagline: Random moves, worse ones sometimes accepted
how: Start from a randomised greedy solution.
Pick a random feasible neighbour (swap, 2-opt, relocate, change a route's depot, split or merge routes).
Accept it if it is better, or if it is worse by an amount d with probability exp(−d / T).
Lower the temperature T step by step; reheat when it has collapsed or nothing was accepted for 500 moves.
refs: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983), Science 220:671–680
impl: A run is many short annealings: after a fixed number of moves it restarts from a new construction. The schedule is not stretched over your time limit.

heuristics.label: Scatter search
heuristics.title: Scatter search
heuristics.tagline: Relink the best solutions in pairs
how: Build a pool of different solutions from random customer orders and improve them.
Keep the best few as the reference set.
Relink every pair in both directions, walking from one customer order toward the other.
Merge the new solutions into the reference set. When it stops changing, build a new pool.
refs: Glover (1977), Decision Sciences 8:156–164
Laguna & Martí (2003), Scatter Search, Kluwer
impl: The reference set is chosen by cost only; there is no distance-based diversity rule.

heuristics.label: Threshold accepting
heuristics.title: Threshold accepting
heuristics.tagline: Accept anything under a shrinking threshold
how: Start from a randomised greedy solution.
Pick a random feasible neighbour.
Accept it if it is not worse than the current solution by more than the threshold. No random draw is involved.
Shrink the threshold a little after every move.
refs: Dueck & Scheuer (1990), Journal of Computational Physics 90:161–175
impl: The threshold starts at a fixed share of the start cost, so it is relative to the instance.

heuristics.label: Tabu search
heuristics.title: Tabu search
heuristics.tagline: Best sampled neighbour, with a memory
how: Start from a randomised greedy solution.
Sample a set of random feasible neighbours.
Move to the best sampled one that is not among the recently visited solutions, even if it is worse than the current one. A tabu solution is allowed if it beats the best ever found.
Remember the new solution; forget the oldest one when the memory is full.
refs: Glover (1989), ORSA Journal on Computing 1:190–206
impl: The memory holds whole solutions, not individual moves, and there is no diversification step.

heuristics.label: Variable neighbourhood search
heuristics.title: Variable neighbourhood search
how: Build a start solution and improve it with local search.
Shake it with k random feasible moves, starting at k = 1.
Improve it; if it beats the current solution, accept it and go back to k = 1. Otherwise raise k, up to a maximum.
After a fixed number of shakes, start again from a new construction.
refs: Mladenović & Hansen (1997), Computers & Operations Research 24:1097–1100
impl: Same random moves as iterated local search, including depot reassignment and route splitting.

operators.title: Move one stop inside its route
operators.short: Take one customer out of the route and put it back at a better place in the same route.
operators.text: The move picks one customer, removes it from the visiting order and tries every other position of the same route. The customers of the route stay the same; only the order changes.
operators.why: Repairs a customer that is reached at the wrong moment, for example one that is passed by on the way and visited later through a detour.
operators.watch: It cannot change which vehicle serves a customer, so it cannot repair a bad split of customers between routes.
refs: Or (1976), Traveling salesman-type combinatorial problems and their relation to the logistics of regional blood banking, PhD thesis, Northwestern University
Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization

operators.title: Move a pair of neighbouring stops inside a route
operators.short: Take two consecutive customers as one block and put the block back elsewhere in the same route.
operators.text: Two customers that are visited one after the other are taken out together and re-inserted, in the same order, at another position of the route.
operators.why: Fixes a small group that belongs together but is visited at the wrong time. Moving the customers one by one would first make the route worse, so the single-stop move does not see it.
operators.watch: The pair keeps its direction; to insert it the other way round you need one of the "reversed" moves between routes or a 2-opt.
refs: Or (1976), Traveling salesman-type combinatorial problems and their relation to the logistics of regional blood banking, PhD thesis, Northwestern University
Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization

operators.title: Swap two stops of a route
operators.short: Exchange the places of two customers of the same route.
operators.text: Two customers of one route, not necessarily neighbours, exchange their positions in the visiting order.
operators.why: Repairs two customers that are visited in each other's place while the stops between them are fine.
operators.watch: If a whole stretch of the route runs in the wrong direction, the 2-opt move is the better tool.
refs: Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization

operators.title: Reverse a stretch of a route (2-opt)
operators.short: Drive a part of the route in the opposite direction; this removes crossings.
operators.text: Two points of the route are chosen and the stretch between them is driven backwards. Two connections are removed and two new ones are added.
operators.why: Removes crossings: when a route crosses itself, reversing the loop makes it shorter. This is the classic move of the travelling-salesman problem.
operators.watch: It never changes which customers a vehicle serves.
refs: Croes (1958), A method for solving traveling-salesman problems, Operations Research 6(6)

operators.title: Give a route to another depot
operators.short: Keep the route as it is, but start and end it at a different depot.
operators.text: The order of the customers does not change. The vehicle simply starts from and returns to another depot. The depot capacity is respected, and if the new depot is not used yet, its opening cost is counted in the comparison.
operators.why: Helpful when a route is served from a far depot while another depot is much closer to its customers.
operators.watch: It changes only the depot of a route; to move single customers use the moves between routes.
refs: Prins, Prodhon & Calvo (2006), Solving the capacitated location-routing problem by a GRASP complemented by a learning process and a path relinking, 4OR 4(3)
Nagy & Salhi (2007), Location-routing: issues, models and methods, European Journal of Operational Research 177(2)

operators.title: Move one customer to another route
operators.short: Take one customer from its route and insert it at the best place of another route.
operators.text: One customer is removed from its route and tried at every position of every other route that still has room for it.
operators.why: Balances the loads, repairs a customer that was given to the wrong vehicle, and can empty a route completely (saving the vehicle cost).
operators.watch: A move is only allowed if the receiving vehicle has enough capacity left.
refs: Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization
Osman (1993), Metastrategy simulated annealing and tabu search algorithms for the vehicle routing problem, Annals of Operations Research 41

operators.title: Move a pair of neighbours to another route
operators.short: Take two consecutive customers and insert them together into another route.
operators.text: Two customers that are visited one after the other move together into another route, in the same order.
operators.why: Moves a small cluster that belongs to another vehicle in one step, where moving the customers one by one would first make the solution worse.
operators.watch: Both customers must fit into the receiving vehicle.
refs: Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization
Osman (1993), Metastrategy simulated annealing and tabu search algorithms for the vehicle routing problem, Annals of Operations Research 41

operators.title: Move a pair to another route, reversed
operators.short: Like the pair move, but the two customers are inserted in the opposite order.
operators.text: Two consecutive customers move to another route and are inserted the other way round.
operators.why: Useful when the second customer of the pair is the one that lies closer to the entry point of the new route.
operators.watch: Only worth the extra scan time if pair moves already help on your data.
refs: Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization

operators.title: Swap one customer between two routes
operators.short: Two customers in different routes exchange their routes.
operators.text: One customer of route A and one customer of route B change places: each is inserted where the other one was.
operators.why: Improves two routes when neither can accept an additional customer (both are nearly full), because the loads stay close to what they were.
operators.watch: Capacity must still hold in both routes after the swap.
refs: Kindervater & Savelsbergh (1997), Vehicle routing: handling edge exchanges, in Local Search in Combinatorial Optimization
Osman (1993), Metastrategy simulated annealing and tabu search algorithms for the vehicle routing problem, Annals of Operations Research 41

operators.title: Swap a pair against one customer
operators.short: Two neighbouring customers of one route are exchanged with a single customer of another route.
operators.text: A pair of consecutive customers of route A is exchanged with one customer of route B (a 2-1 exchange). The numbers of stops of the two routes change by one.
operators.why: Moves two customers one way and one the other way in a single step, which balances routes whose customers have different demands.
operators.watch: One of the more expensive scans between routes.
refs: Osman (1993), Metastrategy simulated annealing and tabu search algorithms for the vehicle routing problem, Annals of Operations Research 41
Taillard et al. (1997), A tabu search heuristic for the vehicle routing problem with soft time windows, Transportation Science 31(2)

operators.title: Swap pairs between two routes
operators.short: Two neighbouring customers of each route are exchanged.
operators.text: A pair of consecutive customers of route A and a pair of consecutive customers of route B change places (a 2-2 exchange).
operators.why: Moves two small groups at once, for example when two neighbouring routes each carry a pair that lies in the other one's area.
operators.watch: One of the more expensive scans between routes.
refs: Osman (1993), Metastrategy simulated annealing and tabu search algorithms for the vehicle routing problem, Annals of Operations Research 41
Taillard et al. (1997), A tabu search heuristic for the vehicle routing problem with soft time windows, Transportation Science 31(2)

operators.title: Swap pairs between routes, reversed
operators.short: Like the pair swap, but each pair is inserted in the opposite order.
operators.text: The two pairs change routes and each pair is turned around on arrival.
operators.why: The orientation of a pair often decides whether it fits the new route well; this move tests it.
operators.watch: One of the more expensive scans between routes.
refs: Taillard et al. (1997), A tabu search heuristic for the vehicle routing problem with soft time windows, Transportation Science 31(2)

operators.title: Exchange the ends of two routes (2-opt*)
operators.short: Cut two routes at one point each and swap their second halves.
operators.text: Each of two routes is cut once. The first part of route A is joined to the second part of route B, and the first part of route B to the second part of route A. Many customers change vehicle at once, but every part keeps its order.
operators.why: Untangles two routes that overlap or cross: the typical situation where single-customer moves cannot help.
operators.watch: The new loads must respect the capacity; the loads of the two routes can become very different.
refs: Potvin & Rousseau (1995), An exchange heuristic for routeing problems with time windows, J. Operational Research Society 46

operators.title: Exchange the ends of two routes, reversed
operators.short: Like 2-opt*, but the swapped halves are driven in reverse.
operators.text: The two routes are cut as in 2-opt*, but each second half is attached backwards.
operators.why: Handles two routes that run towards each other instead of in the same direction.
operators.watch: The most expensive of the route-to-route scans in our measurements.
refs: Potvin & Rousseau (1995), An exchange heuristic for routeing problems with time windows, J. Operational Research Society 46

operators.title: Cut a route in two
operators.short: Split a route at one point; the second part becomes a new route that may start at any depot.
operators.text: A route is cut after some customer. The first part stays; the second part becomes a new route served by a vehicle from any depot.
operators.why: Can pay off when the second part lies near another depot, or when a route has become too long to be sensible.
operators.watch: It adds a vehicle, so the vehicle fixed cost must be smaller than the distance it saves. With a single depot and distances that obey the triangle inequality, cutting a route never shortens the total length.
refs: Prins, Prodhon & Calvo (2006), Solving the capacitated location-routing problem by a GRASP complemented by a learning process and a path relinking, 4OR 4(3)

operators.title: Close a depot
operators.short: Shut one open depot and serve its customers from the other open depots.
operators.text: One open depot is closed. Its customers (largest demand first) are inserted at the cheapest places of the routes of the other open depots, or into new routes at them. The result is tidied up with a few cheap moves before it is compared with the current solution.
operators.why: The opening cost of a depot that serves only a few customers can be larger than the extra distance of serving them from elsewhere. Single-customer moves would have to empty the depot one by one, which looks worse at every step.
operators.watch: An extension that is not part of the main presets Core-5 and Ext-15. Needs room in the other depots.
refs: Nagy & Salhi (2007), Location-routing: issues, models and methods, European Journal of Operational Research 177(2)
Prins, Prodhon & Calvo (2006), Solving the capacitated location-routing problem by a GRASP complemented by a learning process and a path relinking, 4OR 4(3)

operators.title: Move a depot
operators.short: Hand all routes of one depot to another depot; the first closes, the second opens.
operators.text: Every route of depot A is given to depot B (open or closed). A closes and B opens or absorbs the routes. The routes are then tidied up with a few cheap moves.
operators.why: Relocates a facility in one step: the old site closes, the new site opens, and the cost comparison includes both opening costs.
operators.watch: By far the most expensive scan in the list, up to hundreds of times slower than the route moves. An extension that is not part of the main presets.
refs: Nagy & Salhi (2007), Location-routing: issues, models and methods, European Journal of Operational Research 177(2)
Prins, Prodhon & Calvo (2006), Solving the capacitated location-routing problem by a GRASP complemented by a learning process and a path relinking, 4OR 4(3)

operators.title: Open a new depot
operators.short: Open a closed depot near a group of customers and rebuild their routes from it.
operators.text: A closed depot is opened. The customers nearest to it (enough for one, two or three vehicle loads, within the depot capacity) are taken out of their routes and rebuilt into new routes at the new depot. The result is tidied up with a few cheap moves.
operators.why: A new depot close to a dense group of customers can replace many long trips from far away. The opening cost is counted in the comparison.
operators.watch: Very expensive scan. An extension that is not part of the main presets.
refs: Nagy & Salhi (2007), Location-routing: issues, models and methods, European Journal of Operational Research 177(2)
Prins, Prodhon & Calvo (2006), Solving the capacitated location-routing problem by a GRASP complemented by a learning process and a path relinking, 4OR 4(3)

operator_groups.title: Inside one route
operator_groups.blurb: These moves only change the order of stops of a single vehicle. The set of customers of every route stays the same.

operator_groups.title: Between two routes
operator_groups.blurb: These moves hand customers from one vehicle to another. The vehicle capacity is always respected.

operator_groups.title: Whole routes
operator_groups.blurb: These moves treat a route as one block: which depot serves it, or whether it should be cut in two.

operator_groups.title: Depot decisions
operator_groups.blurb: These moves change which depots are open. They are far more expensive to scan than the others, but they are the only moves that can close or open a depot in one step.

none.title: No local search
none.text: The method uses only its own moves. Choose this to see the method on its own.
steps: The method builds and changes solutions with its own rules.

first.title: First improvement
first.text: Walk through the chosen operators in the order you gave. As soon as a move makes the solution cheaper, apply it and start again from the first operator. Fast and simple; the engine implements it for only five operators, the Base-5 set (the others are greyed out).
steps: Try operator 1: is there any move that lowers the cost?
If yes, apply the first one found and go back to operator 1.
If no, try operator 2, and so on.
Stop when no operator finds a better move.

vnd.title: Variable neighbourhood descent (VND)
vnd.text: Use the operators one after the other in the order you gave. An operator is scanned completely and its best move is applied; after any improvement the search goes back to the first operator. Put the cheap operators first and the expensive ones last.
steps: Scan operator 1 completely and take its best move if it lowers the cost.
After an improvement go back to operator 1; otherwise go on to operator 2.
Repeat until no operator finds an improvement.

rvnd.title: Randomised VND
rvnd.text: Like VND, but the order of the operators is shuffled (and reshuffled after every improvement). It avoids favouring one order and gives different results for different seeds.
steps: Scan the first one; if it improves, apply the move and shuffle the full list again.
If it does not, drop it from the list for now.
Stop when the list is empty.

best.title: Best improvement over all
best.text: Scan every chosen operator completely, then apply the single best move found by any of them, and repeat. Each step is slower, but it always takes the steepest descent.
steps: Pick the move with the largest cost reduction.
Stop when no operator finds an improvement.

restarts_per_depot_subset.label: Constructions per pass
restarts_per_depot_subset.plain_help: Randomised constructions GRASP makes before a new pass starts.

alpha.help: legacy value-RCL alpha; ignored in cardinality mode
alpha.label: Value-based list width
alpha.plain_help: Legacy setting; ignored while the candidate-list rule is cardinality.

rcl_mode.label: Candidate-list rule
rcl_mode.plain_help: cardinality: choose at random among the k best insertion moves. value: legacy threshold rule.

rcl_max.label: Longest candidate list
rcl_max.plain_help: The randomised construction draws among the 1 to this many best insertion moves.

depot_mode.label: Depot subsets
depot_mode.plain_help: How subsets of depots are listed. With all depots allowed there is one subset, so this has no visible effect.

depot_sample.label: Sampled depot subsets
depot_sample.plain_help: Used only when depot subsets are sampled.

depot_layer.help: none | halving (successive halving over candidate depot sets)
depot_layer.label: Depot-set search
depot_layer.plain_help: Which depots to open is normally decided inside each method. "halving" first tries several depot sets on short runs and keeps the winners (successive halving). "none" is the standard behaviour of the engine.

layer_sets.help: candidate depot sets at the first rung
layer_sets.label: Depot sets to try
layer_sets.plain_help: How many candidate depot sets the first round of the depot-set search compares (the set of all depots is always one of them).

layer_eta.label: Halving factor
layer_eta.plain_help: After each round only 1/factor of the depot sets survive. With 8 sets and factor 2 the rounds have 8, 4, 2 and 1 sets.

layer_probe_frac.help: share of the time budget for the probe solution
layer_probe_frac.label: Time share of the first probe
layer_probe_frac.plain_help: Share of the time budget spent on one quick solution that suggests which depots look useful.

reference_tol.label: Reference tolerance
reference_tol.plain_help: In objective units, not percent. A run counts as reaching the reference when its objective is at most the reference plus this value.

vns_kmax.label: Largest shake size
vns_kmax.plain_help: Number of random moves of the strongest shake.

sa_iters.label: Moves per annealing
sa_iters.plain_help: After this many moves the search restarts from a new construction.

sa_cooling.label: Cooling factor per move
sa_cooling.plain_help: The temperature is multiplied by this after every move.

sa_reheat.label: Reheat level
sa_reheat.plain_help: Share of the start temperature restored when the temperature has collapsed.

tabu_tenure.label: Memory length
tabu_tenure.plain_help: Number of recent solutions that are forbidden.

ga_generations.label: Generations
ga_generations.plain_help: Applies to the fixed-trials budget only.

ga_elite.label: Elite solutions kept
ga_elite.plain_help: Copied unchanged into the next generation.

alns_reaction.label: Weight reaction factor
alns_reaction.plain_help: How fast operator weights follow their recent scores.

brkga_generations.label: Generations
brkga_generations.plain_help: Applies to the fixed-trials budget only.

brkga_mutant_frac.label: Mutant share
brkga_mutant_frac.plain_help: Fresh random vectors added every generation.
